threads.title: Agones on your own cloud or managed hosting for dedicated servers?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
Once a game outgrows peer-to-peer or a single rented box, someone has to run fleets of dedicated servers. Do you operate Kubernetes yourself with an open source tool, or pay a managed platform to handle allocation and regions?

The Agones homepage describes it as an open source platform to host, run and scale dedicated game servers on Kubernetes, and as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox project. The Edgegap pricing page shows a managed alternative billed by the minute on usage, with a free trial, which is one example of how managed pricing is structured.

Share what your traffic looks like (spiky or steady), how many regions you cover and who on the team carries the pager. Reports of costs or outages you hit are welcome, with as much specificity as you are able to share.

threads.title: Git LFS or Perforce for a project with heavy binary assets?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
Texture, audio and scene files make ordinary Git awkward, and teams usually end up choosing between Git with large-file support, Perforce or a newer cloud tool. What did you choose, and how did file locking and repository size behave over time?

The Git LFS homepage describes it as an open source Git extension for keeping large files on a remote server, keeping the same Git workflow and access controls. The Perforce product page describes P4 as a version control platform for code and large digital assets, and says it is free for up to 5 users and 20 workspaces. The Diversion homepage describes a version control platform for very large repositories with Unreal Engine, Unity and Perforce migration support.

Tell us your engine, team size and the point at which your first choice started to hurt. Experience with migrating between systems is especially useful.

threads.title: Godot or Unity for a first commercial 2D game in 2026?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
A solo developer or a team of two is about to commit to an engine for a first commercial 2D game, and the choice is hard to reverse once art, code and tooling pile up. Which of Godot and Unity are you picking, and what decided it?

Two facts from the vendors themselves frame the choice. The Godot homepage calls it a free, open-source 2D and 3D game engine and makes no other pricing statement. The Unity homepage says you can get started for free or find a plan, and lists desktop, iOS, Android, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation, Xbox, Meta Quest, web and Apple Vision Pro as platforms, without showing plan figures.

Console and mobile reach, asset store dependence, scripting language preference and how much you trust a license to stay stable all tend to matter more than raw 2D features. If you shipped or abandoned a 2D project in either engine, share what the deciding factor was and what you would check earlier next time.

threads.title: Kernel anti-cheat: worth the player backlash?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
Kernel-level anti-cheat can catch cheats that operate deep in the operating system, but players and security researchers often object to software with that level of access. Where do you draw the line for a competitive game, and what does your community tolerate?

Vendors present their offerings differently. The Easy Anti-Cheat site lists support for Windows, Mac, Linux and Steam Deck and says integration is self-service through the Epic Online Services SDK, with basic protection free. The BattlEye homepage describes the service as independent anti-cheat that updates protection against new exploits and permanently bans cheaters.

Server-side detection, authoritative servers and report-and-review systems are alternatives or complements. If you have weighed these for a launch, or decided to leave a protection layer out, share your reasoning, including what you told players about it.

threads.title: RTMP or SRT for sending the feed from a remote location?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
RTMP is accepted almost everywhere, while SRT promises better recovery on shaky links. If you send a feed from a venue, a mobile connection or a second site, which protocol do you use and what is on the receiving end?

Many open source servers handle both: the MediaMTX repository lists SRT, WebRTC, RTSP, RTMP, LL-HLS, MPEG-TS and RTP, and the SRS site lists RTMP, WebRTC, HLS, HTTP-FLV, SRT and MPEG-DASH. Whether a platform accepts SRT directly or only RTMP decides how many hops you need.

Share your link type (wired, bonded cellular, satellite), what loss you saw and how you tuned latency settings.

threads.title: What bitrate and encoder settings do you stream at?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
Streamers swap settings constantly: encoder, bitrate, keyframe interval, resolution and frame rate. What do you run for a fast game, and did you change it after a drop in viewers or a platform update?

YouTube's live encoder help page lists a recommended bitrate of 17 Mbps for 1080p at 60 frames per second with H.264, and 12 Mbps for the same resolution with AV1 or H.265. It recommends a keyframe frequency of 2 seconds, says not to exceed 4 seconds, and lists CBR as the bitrate encoding.

Other platforms publish their own limits, and your upload speed and hardware encoder set the real ceiling. Post your platform, encoder (software or hardware), resolution and what you changed that made a visible difference.

threads.title: Welcome to the GA Forum boards: how this forum works
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
GA Forum is a discussion space for game developers, streamers, esports organizers and corporate live-video teams. The boards are Games, Livestreaming, Esports and General, and each is meant for practical questions about tools, workflows and trade-offs.

Posting rules: be civil and critique ideas, not people. If you work for a vendor or have a financial interest in a tool you mention, say so in the post. New accounts' posts that contain links are reviewed before they appear, so a short delay is normal. Do not post stream keys, API secrets or private contact details.

Our rankings and guides are written by the editorial team and sourced from vendor pages; read how in the editorial process. Starter threads on the boards were opened by the editorial team to get conversations going and contain no replies from users. Introduce your project or ask your first question on the board that fits.

threads.title: When in development do you open a Steam playtest?
threads.author: GA Forum editorial team
threads.body_html:
Opening a playtest too early wastes the interest of people who might wishlist, and too late leaves no time to act on feedback. At what stage of your build do you start inviting outside players, and how do you pick who gets in?

The Steamworks documentation describes Steam Playtest as a free way for developers to get playtesting data, and says charging customers for access is not allowed. It also notes that developers can request more than 50,000 playtest keys, but Valve reviews such requests case by case and may reject them.

Paid services recruit and record testers instead, such as the one described on the PlaytestCloud home page. Share how you combine community playtests with structured sessions, what you track and what you changed because of it.
